title: Record-Breaking Cosmic Blast Kept Flaring for 27 Days
summary:
Astronomers have found a cosmic explosion that refused to quit. The blast, called GRB 220706A, was first spotted on July 6, 2022, and its central engine kept flaring in X-rays for around 27 days.

That is about 20 days longer than the previous record for this kind of delayed flaring, which was about six days. Gamma-ray bursts, or GRBs, are among the most powerful explosions in the cosmos.

Long GRBs have been linked to the collapse of a massive star, which also triggers a supernova and creates a black hole. GRB 220706A is an ultra-long GRB, a rare type in which the engine stays active for longer, and its cause is still unknown.

Study team member Benjamin Gompertz, of the University of Birmingham in England, said X-ray flaring after a GRB is common, but it had always come within the first few days. Seeing flaring at around 27 days in the burst's rest frame, he said, tells scientists that an ongoing active process is at work, which is unprecedented in the known population.

Gompertz said the team does not know what central engine is driving this outburst, and that mystery is what makes the event so compelling. The supernova tells scientists that a star collapsed, the standard power source for GRBs, but that alone does not immediately explain the extremely late flaring or the unusually bright supernova.

One possibility is a magnetar, a neutron star with a particularly powerful magnetic field. Gompertz said the new supernova looks a lot like the one linked to another ultra-long GRB from 2011, GRB 111209A, which was determined to be powered by a magnetar.
why_it_matters: This record-breaking burst challenges what scientists thought they knew about how cosmic explosions power themselves, and solving its mystery could reshape their picture of collapsing stars and the engines they leave behind.
